newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - Japan looking at Brazilian beans.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Japan looking at Brazilian beans.

text.p: Japanese traders said on Monday they are increasingly interested in the cheaper Brazilian soybean crop as buyers continue to purchase U.S. soybeans for February shipment ahead of the Christmas holidays.

"Japan already bought up to 160,000 tonnes of Brazilian soybeans for shipments after next April. The Brazilian crop has higher protein than the U.S. and has no quality problems," a soybean trader said.
The elimination of Brazil's export tax on grains helped boost Japanese interest in the South American crop, traders said.
Brazil in mid-September lifted the state export tax on primary and semi-manufactured goods. Soybeans were subject previously to a 13 percent tax, soymeal 11.1 percent and soyoil 8.0 percent.
Japanese buying of U.S. soybeans continued, the traders said.
"We'd like to cover U.S. soybeans for nearly 50 percent of February shipment by the end of next week," a soybean trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Japanese premiums for U.S. soybeans are currently quoted at around 130 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade's (CBOT) March contract.
Japanese buying in the world corn market, however, will remain limited this week, traders said.
"Some would buy small amount of U.S. corn this week for the January-March shipment, but many are waiting for further price drops," a corn trader said.
Argentine corn will be more popular for Japanese feed makers during April-June 1997 shipment, traders said.
Some trading houses are gradually stepping up corn import talks for 1997 with Argentina following a grain mission to the country.
"Corn imports from Argentina may be accelerated next year," a corn trader said.
In the Philippines, two flour companies bought 35,000 tonnes of Canadian wheat at a price below US$195 a tonne FOB Pacific Northwest.
Manila flour companies found U.S. wheat expensive and were now considering alternative supplies from Canada, Australia and Argentina.
"The offers for the U.S. wheat were too high. We are looking now at Canadian wheat as an alternative as prices are more reasonable," a trader said.

Taiwanese traders said on Monday they may tender for one shipment of 54,000 tonnes of U.S. corn and soybeans. Most of the other buyers appeared willing to wait for prices to hit bottom before placing tenders.
"We are not sure if the corn and soybean futures prices will drop lower, so we can just wait and see," a buyer said.
The Taiwan Flour Mills Association, which recently bought 72,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat last week, will remain sidelined this week, association spokesman Lu Wei-chih said.

Freight cost from the Pacific Northwest was about US$11.50 per tonne while rates from the Gulf of Mexico ranged between US$20.50-$21.50 a tonne, both for Panamax-sized March shipments. In Seoul, traders said South Korean corn processors would likely retain a low profile this week unless a major change occurs in the prospects for international prices.
"Most Korean processors have enough amount booked for well into the middle of next year and there's no reason for them to hurry up," said one trader.
They said corn was trading at around $140 per tonne C&F, and processors saw room for prices to go down further.
"I think there will be no major activity among Korean corn buyers until the middle of January," the trader said.
